chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad narrated from Ali ibn al-Nu'man, from Ibn Muskān, from al-'Alā' al-Sābiriyyah (the merchant of Sābir) who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a woman who deposited wealth with a man. When death approached her, she said to him, 'The wealth that I gave you is for so-and-so.' The woman died, and her heirs came to the man and said to him, 'There was wealth belonging to our companion; we do not see it except with you, so swear to us that there is nothing with you.' He asked, 'Should he swear to them?' He (peace be upon him) said, 'If she was trustworthy in his eyes, he should swear to them; and if she was suspected (of having taken some), he should not swear and should leave the matter as it was, for only one-third of her wealth is hers.'

key_terms.مُتَّهَمَةً: suspected (of dishonesty or consuming part of the deposit)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on a deposit made during final illness if the depositor is suspected of having consumed part of it?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* clarifies the evidentiary standards for debt repayment during the final illness (*marad al-mawt*), a critical period where a person's intent to distribute wealth is scrutinized. It establishes that the custodian's oath is contingent upon the depositor's known financial habits: a trustworthy (*ma'mūnah*) woman’s claim is accepted fully upon oath, whereas a suspected (*muttahamah*) one results in a presumption of consumption, limiting the heirs' recovery to two-thirds of the deposit. This ruling highlights the Shia juristic emphasis on the custodian's personal knowledge and the presumption of continuity (*istishab*) in financial transactions.
